awd_titl_txt: Conference: CI PAOS: Challenges and Opportunities of Research Data Management in Construction Engineering
awd_abstract_narration:
A workshop is planned to promote research data management (RDM) in the construction research community. The construction industry is experiencing an array of challenges including low productivity, issues in safety performance, and shortage of skilled workforce. To address these challenges, the construction research community has put much effort into integrating automation technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, and Internet of Things (IoT) to support infrastructure management, on-site safety control, and structure health monitoring. 

Through collaboration between construction engineering and cyberinfrastructure experts, this project team will organize and hold a two-day workshop in May 2026 at the Michigan Tech University campus to identify challenges and opportunities of RDM in the construction research community. The workshop will invite leading scholars from government, industry and academia, including early-career researchers, and journal editors from construction engineering, open science, and cyberinfrastructure venues. The workshop facilitates the digital transformation of the construction industry by building the scientific connection between construction and open science communities, which will support construction community involvement and contribute to the Nation’s cyberinfrastructure ecosystem.

This award by the Office of Advanced Cyberinfrastructure is jointly supported by the Directorate for Engineering.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The growing use of digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) in construction research has increased the need for reliable, accessible, and reusable research data. Construction projects generate diverse information across different activities, organizations, and software systems, but managing and sharing these resources for broader research use remains challenging. This award supported the 2026 NSF Workshop on Research Data Management in Construction Engineering: Challenges and Opportunities to examine these needs and bring together construction research, open science, and computing infrastructure communities.

The workshop took place on May 7–8, 2026, at Michigan Technological University in Houghton, Michigan. It brought together more than 40 participants from over 15 U.S. states, including academic researchers, educators, industry professionals, and computing infrastructure experts. Before the workshop, a survey gathered feedback on current data management practices and potential discussion topics to inform program planning. The two-day program included 10 invited presentations, two panel discussions, and a breakout session organized around four discussion topics.

The presentations and discussions addressed four interconnected areas. The first concerned technical and social challenges in preparing and reusing construction data, including limited reliable annotations, inconsistent data structures, insufficient evaluation benchmarks, and barriers to accessing industry-held information. The second examined best practices and ethics, including data quality, documentation, licensing, and the effort required to maintain datasets after publication. Particular attention was given to privacy concerns involving video recordings, behavioral information, and physiological measurements. The third explored data security, trusted sharing, and long-term management. The fourth examined collaboration among universities, industry partners, government agencies, and research communities, including differences in priorities, data ownership, and incentives to contribute data.

The workshop findings highlighted several gaps between current practices and the requirements for reliable and reusable research data. Data collected for one construction project or research task may not be suitable for another without additional validation and contextual information. Publishing datasets improves access, but continued reuse requires maintenance, documentation, and user support. Records of data processing do not necessarily establish the authenticity of the original information. Protecting sensitive information after sharing also remains difficult, while the costs, risks, and benefits of contributing data are often unevenly distributed.

The resulting report recommends developing reusable datasets and evaluation benchmarks around clearly defined research needs; strengthening data verification and appropriate sharing practices; clarifying responsibilities for long-term maintenance; and organizing collaboration around specific outputs, such as documented datasets, practical guidance, and shared benchmarks. These recommendations identify directions for future work rather than completed technical solutions. The project provided opportunities for participants from different disciplines and organizations to exchange experiences and discuss common research needs. Its findings and recommendations were documented in a publicly accessible workshop report. Workshop information and available presentation materials are accessible through the workshop website, providing resources for researchers, educators, and others interested in responsible data management and reuse in construction.
